The Thyroid Deception:

Underactive thyroid as the hidden cause of hair loss – even when your “blood tests look perfect”

From hair loss to hair fullness in just 5 months: How I finally regained thick, healthy hair after 5 years of despair.

Hannah Collins| Thyroid Specialist

Written on 24/04/2025

The hairbrush was full of hair again – just like every morning.

The same picture in the shower: handfuls of hair in the drain.

And every time I looked in the mirror, I knew it was getting worse.

At some point, I didn’t recognise myself anymore.

Not just because my hair had become thinner, drier, weaker.

But because I felt like I had lost myself.

I was exhausted, irritable, unfocused.

I slept eight hours – and woke up feeling as if I’d run a marathon during the night.

My GP kept saying: “Your blood tests are fine. That’s normal for your age.”

But deep down, I knew something wasn’t right.

I felt like a stranger in my own life.

And no one took me seriously.

Hello, I’m Hannah, and my hair loss began around five years ago.

It started gradually.

A few more hairs in the brush than usual.

Nothing to worry about, I thought at the time.

We all lose hair. That’s normal.

But month after month, more and more hair stayed behind in my brush.

I had to clean the shower drain every day.

My ponytail, once thick and full, suddenly felt thin and lifeless.

One evening, I pulled out an old photo album.

There I was, ten years ago, with thick, shiny hair.

I held the photo next to my reflection and burst into tears.

How could I have lost so much hair?

I started trying everything possible to get my old hair back:

Expensive caffeine and biotin shampoos.

Hair supplements that cost a fortune.

Even a pricey scalp serum recommended by a friend.

Nothing worked.

The hair loss got worse.

And with it came exhaustion, concentration problems, and dry skin.

Only when I started researching more deeply did I stumble upon the real reason behind my hair loss: my thyroid.

I had been diagnosed with an underactive thyroid nine years earlier.

I took my L-Thyroxine diligently every morning.

And at every check-up, my GP reassured me: “Your blood tests are perfectly adjusted.”

So how was it possible that I was still suffering so badly?

That I was losing my hair even though my results looked “perfect”?

What I didn’t know back then: the hair loss, the fatigue, the irritability, the focus problems — they all had the same root cause.

And that cause had nothing to do with my age, my genes or bad shampoos.

It lay within an overlooked mechanism in my body.

A vital process that must take place for thyroid hormones to work at all.

Looking back now, equipped with today’s knowledge, everything finally made sense.

Within a few months, not only had I stopped my hair loss…

I began to regrow hair.

Baby hairs that finally covered my scalp again.

My existing hair became stronger, shinier, more vibrant.

But that wasn’t all.

My energy returned.

My concentration.

My joy.

I felt like myself again.

When I shared my new approach with a few friends who had also been struggling with thyroid problems for years, something amazing happened:

They reported the same changes. More energy. Less hair loss. A new sense of life.

That’s when I realised: I’m not alone with this. Thousands of people suffer in silence, without knowing there is a solution.

That’s why I wanted to share my story – because I want to help you too.

No one should be sitting in a corner today, feeling lost, and suffering quietly.

Understand your blood results – before they continue to mislead you

I was sitting at the GP’s surgery again.

Tired, exhausted, dealing with hair loss, dry skin and completely drained.

Once again, I had blood taken – just as I had countless times before.

The tests carried out were:

– the TSH level

– the fT4 level

Sounds medical? It is – but I’m going to explain exactly what you need to know.

What exactly is the TSH level?

The TSH level determines how many thyroid hormones the body should produce.

The higher the TSH level, the more thyroid hormones your body is missing.

Almost all doctors test the TSH level.

What is the fT4 level?

The fT4 level (free thyroxine) measures the amount of T4 in your blood – the inactive thyroid hormone.

This is exactly the hormone you are given as medication (e.g. L-Thyroxine).

The blood test my GP carried out

My GP correctly identified that my TSH level was elevated.

My fT4 was too low.

At the time, I didn’t understand the values.

But my GP knew – and that mattered.

I was told: “The higher the TSH level, the fewer thyroid hormones are available.”

In my case, my TSH level was 3.1!

Because of this, I received the diagnosis of an underactive thyroid from my GP straight away.

After the diagnosis, I felt relieved at first.

I wasn’t completely in the dark anymore.

At least I had an explanation for my hair loss.

My GP gave me hope that things would improve.

After all, I wasn’t the only one dealing with this.

With correct adjustment of the medication, everything should return to normal and the symptoms should disappear.

That brings us to the topic of “correctly adjusting” your medication.

If you also suffer from an underactive thyroid, you’ll know this situation well:

Your GP prescribes L-Thyroxine – the standard treatment for thyroid problems.

My GP initially prescribed 25 micrograms of L-Thyroxine.

L-Thyroxine, an artificially produced thyroid hormone, is the most commonly prescribed medication after painkillers in the South Africa.

“You’re correctly adjusted again now — your thyroid should function as normal.”

Full of hope, I went to the pharmacy, collected my thyroid medication, and took it for a while.

Somehow nothing changed, except that swallowing the tablets became part of my morning routine.

A month later, the GP increased the dose from 25 to 50 micrograms.

I went back to the GP and heard:

“Hello Mrs Langford, your blood results have improved a lot.”

Yes, my blood results were great.

And I did actually feel better.

But only for a few months.

The hair loss gets worse

Five months after my diagnosis, my husband asked me:

“What good are your ‘great blood results’ if your hair loss isn’t improving?”

He was right.

Since the increase in my dose and taking the medication regularly, not only had my hair loss got worse, but so had my other symptoms.

I had gained 5kg — without changing anything in my diet.

And the constant fatigue?

It persisted stubbornly, just like the hair loss.

So I began searching for other solutions.

Dr Bennett explained how thyroid hormones really work, what TSH, T4 and T3 actually are, and much more.

I will try to summarise it for you as clearly as possible.

The difference between T4 and T3

There are two thyroid hormones that matter: T4 and T3 (sometimes also written as fT4 and fT3).

Our thyroid produces around 80% T4 and 20% T3.

With an underactive thyroid, the gland no longer produces enough T4 and T3.

As a result, you are prescribed tablets such as L-Thyroxine.

These tablets are meant to replace the missing hormones.

Dr Bennett wasn’t impressed.

He told me: giving L-Thyroxine alone doesn’t work, because it’s only T4.

T4 is the inactive thyroid hormone.

It is simply a storage form — not active in the body.

T3, however, is the active thyroid hormone that supplies every organ with energy.

T4 must be converted into T3 in the body — activated.

Only when this conversion from T4 to T3 works can the cells produce energy properly.

Then we have energy, we’re no longer exhausted, and — drumroll — hair becomes thick and full again.

The connection between hair loss and an underactive thyroid is explained in detail in this study

How your thyroid influences your hair growth

The active thyroid hormone T3 is one of the most essential hormones in the body.

Why? Because it provides energy to every cell.

When we have enough T3, we’re not cold, our metabolism runs faster, we have more energy and both our gut and scalp are better supplied with blood.

In short: T3 controls how fast numerous metabolic processes run in the body — including hair growth.

Normally, each hair goes through three phases:

Growth phase, transition phase, and resting phase.

Without enough T3, the hair stays far too long in the resting phase — meaning:

It falls out, but doesn’t grow back.

The same applies to nails: people with an underactive thyroid often have brittle nails that grow slowly.

Vertical ridges in fingernails are also a commonly overlooked sign of hypothyroidism.

Both hair and nail growth rely heavily on the protein keratin.

Keratin is the main building block of our hair and nails.

And to produce keratin, the body needs energy — meaning T3.

If T3 is missing, keratin cannot be produced.

Hair becomes thinner, breaks easily and barely regrows.

Nails become brittle, and the risk of nail fungus increases.

The natural hair cycle becomes disrupted.

After all of Dr Bennett’s explanations, I finally understood why the shampoos, vitamins and ampoules hadn’t worked.

As long as my body wasn’t producing active T3, my hair stood no chance.

Why thyroid medication doesn’t work

I now understood: T3 is the important thyroid hormone.

Exactly — T3, the value my GP didn’t even measure at the beginning!

Dr Collins explained to me: “You’ve only been taking T4 medication so far. But your body has to convert T4 into T3, otherwise symptoms like hair loss won’t stop.”

Thyroid activation consists of three simple steps:

  1. Production of thyroid hormones (T4)

  2. Conversion of T4 into its active form, T3

  3. Transport of T3 to the cells

Most doctors only focus on step 1 by prescribing synthetic hormones such as Levothyroxine.

This makes the blood values look good again (doctors assume they’ve done their job), especially the TSH and T4 values.

But the symptoms often don’t go away.

Your GP then tells you that you’re “well adjusted” because your T4 and TSH look fine.

But if you are still constantly tired, experiencing hair loss, concentration problems, cold hands, digestive issues, and your metabolism is so slow that you gain weight just by looking at a slice of cake — then in most cases, it comes down to one thing:

A conversion disorder.

When Dr Collins explained all this to me, it was the first time in 15 years that I felt understood — and properly informed.

Slowly the puzzle pieces fitted together, and Dr Collins showed me that my hair loss could only have come from the fact that the inactive T4 from the tablets was not being converted into active T3.

I was suffering from a conversion disorder.

The thyroid deception

What goes wrong with traditional treatment:

❌ Too many doctors look only at TSH and T4, and completely ignore T3.

❌ Treatment is based on blood values, not symptoms. If TSH and T4 look normal, the GP insists everything is fine.

❌ They stubbornly continue prescribing synthetic T4 and keep increasing the dose even though symptoms persist.

The connection between the thyroid and the liver

After diagnosing me with a conversion disorder, Dr Collins explained the crucial role of the liver.

Up to 80% of thyroid hormones are converted inside the liver.

Has a doctor ever explained to you that the thyroid and liver are deeply connected?

Step one: the inactive T4 is taken up by the liver cells.

Inside these cells are the enzymes (deiodinases) responsible for the conversion.

These enzymes remove one iodine atom from the outer ring of the T4 molecule.

This transforms T4 into T3 (the active thyroid hormone).

You can imagine it like this:

The T4 cannot be converted in the liver

Normally, the enzymes have no difficulty removing the iodine atom from T4.

But in many people with a conversion disorder, the deiodinase enzymes don’t function properly.

The T4 taken through medication can only be converted into T3 at a very low rate.

As a result, your dose keeps increasing.

Imagine a sink where the drain becomes more and more blocked.

The solution is not to pour in more water.

The solution is to unblock the drain so the water can flow again.

According to Dr Collins, two problems must be solved.

Problem #1: The overburdened liver

Liver cells don’t only convert T4 into T3.

The liver is the main organ responsible for removing toxins from the body.

Toxins include exhaust fumes, smoke, plastics, electromagnetic pollution, pesticides, and heavy metals.

Years of medication and an unhealthy diet also weaken the liver.

And just like we prioritise tasks each day, the liver also prioritises.

Recent estimates suggest that one in four people in South Africa now suffers from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Cholesterol is often elevated as well.

And yes — years of taking Levothyroxine certainly do not make the liver’s job easier.

Medication weakens the liver, and a sluggish liver makes you feel sluggish.

It becomes a vicious cycle.

We take a drug hoping to feel better, yet at the same time we accept its side effects — which weaken our organs.

Strange, isn’t it, when you really think about it?

Can you imagine what state my liver would be in if I continued taking Levothyroxine every day for the next 20 years?

Yes, thyroid hormones have their place in treatment.

And it makes no sense to suddenly stop them overnight.

But they should never be the only strategy for life.

The body must eventually be encouraged to produce, convert and transport hormones on its own again.

If this doesn’t happen, you remain trapped in the “thyroxine cycle” forever.

Besides an overworked liver, there is another problem that is almost always ignored.

Problem #2: Missing nutrients needed for conversion

We now know that thyroid hormone conversion happens mostly in the liver.

The conversion process is called 5’-deiodinase.

These deiodinase enzymes remove an iodine atom from T4, turning it into T3.

For these enzymes to function properly, they need nutrients such as zinc and iron.

But the most important nutrient is selenium, which is a structural component of these enzymes.

Without enough selenium, the conversion simply does not work. (1)

Study shows: Selenium deficiency can cause conversion disorders

A study showed: patients with a selenium deficiency had high T4 levels but very low T3 levels — meaning a conversion disorder.

Now comes the big problem:

The soil in many regions of South Africa is selenium-poor, just like in central.

This means our locally produced food contains very little selenium.

It’s estimated that most people in South Africa do not get sufficient selenium from their diet.

Therefore, supporting selenium levels is essential — through diet or supplementation.

Summary so far

✅ Your body needs the active thyroid hormone T3 — only then symptoms like hair loss, fatigue or weight gain improve.

✅ Thyroid medication like Levothyroxine provides only inactive T4.

✅ The conversion from T4 into T3 happens mainly in the liver.

✅ If symptoms persist despite medication, it is very likely a conversion disorder.

✅ Increasing the medication dose is NOT the solution.

Step 2: Micronutrients for conversion

There are two key nutrients that play a direct role in converting T4 into T3 inside the liver: selenium and glutathione.

Selenium

I have already written a lot about selenium.

Selenium is directly involved in hormone conversion in the liver — because the enzymes that convert T4 to T3 are made from selenium.

But selenium can do even more.

As a co-factor, it also plays a role in the production of thyroid hormones.

Selenium is an absolute must for anyone with an underactive thyroid.

Glutathione

Glutathione is the most abundant and one of the most powerful antioxidants in the body.

In its active form, it can neutralise free radicals.

Normally, glutathione captures these free radicals and protects our cells.

But when there are too many free radicals, glutathione becomes depleted.

Scientifically, we say that glutathione becomes “oxidised” (used up).

Once depleted, it can no longer help — and the cells and their energy centres become more vulnerable to damage.

Studies show that people with Hashimoto’s, for example, have less than half the amount of glutathione (GSH) in their serum compared to healthy individuals (4).

Yes, you read that correctly:

Less than half the glutathione!

This is why it is so important to supply glutathione to restore the balance between oxidative stress and antioxidants.

No doctor ever mentioned glutathione to me — even though the research is crystal clear.

But that’s not all:

Glutathione, alongside selenium, directly influences the conversion of T4 to T3.

This was shown in the following study:

Researchers found that people with impaired conversion almost always had low glutathione levels (5).

Glutathione is therefore a crucial nutrient that most people lack for optimal hormone conversion.

It is also one of the blood values that most doctors overlook and rarely test.

Dr Andrew Collins explained it like this:

🚨 Too little energy (T3) for your liver = high cholesterol levels because cholesterol breakdown in the liver no longer functions properly

🚨 Too little T3 = slow metabolism, making it almost impossible to manage your weight

🚨 Too little T3 for your gut = digestive issues because your gut is no longer properly supplied with blood

🚨 Too little T3 = constantly cold hands & feet because your body has reduced circulation

🚨 Too little T3 = higher risk of developing diabetes because, with a lack of T3, the gene expression for the glucose transport protein decreases. The result: blood sugar rises more quickly

🚨 Too little T3 = the receptor for the sleep hormone melatonin becomes downregulated, making good sleep more difficult

🚨 Too little T3 = the receptor for the happiness hormone serotonin becomes downregulated. A lack of T3 can therefore lead to depression.

🚨 Too little T3 = the luteinising hormone (LH), which stimulates ovulation, becomes downregulated. This is why a T3 deficiency can also be a cause of infertility.

🚨 Too little T3 = calcitonin, the hormone that governs calcium storage in the bones, becomes downregulated. A lack of T3 therefore causes bone loss (osteoporosis)

Additional notes:

Since publishing this article, many of you have asked questions. So here are the most important answers:

Who is BioEdge™ suitable for?

If one or more of these apply to you, BioEdge™ will very likely help:

  • You already take thyroid medication but feel no improvement

  • Your free T4 is fine, but your free T3 is very low

  • Your reverse T3 is very high

  • You have a fatty liver or very weak liver function. Signs may include: pressure in the upper abdomen, night-time urination, yellowish discolouration of eyes, stool or urine, bloating, fullness, loss of appetite

  • You have high cholesterol and/or triglyceride levels

  • You have little or no remaining thyroid tissue and rely on thyroid medication

Can I take BioEdge™ if I no longer have a thyroid?

Yes, absolutely. BioEdge™ contains only natural ingredients. Especially if you no longer have a thyroid, it’s even more important that the T4 you take can be converted more effectively.

Can I take BioEdge™ if I have Hashimoto’s?

Yes, it makes perfect sense to support your body with hormone conversion. People with Hashimoto’s often struggle even more with chronic inflammation and oxidative stress.

How can BioEdge™ help with weight loss?

Simple: weight issues are usually caused by a slow metabolism.

Metabolic problems – like most symptoms – come from too little active thyroid hormone reaching your cells.

By improving the conversion of T4 to T3, your metabolism improves too.

Should I continue taking my thyroid medication?

Yes, definitely! Please don’t stop your medication. BioEdge™ is not a medication for hypothyroidism.

The manufacturer recommends taking BioEdge™ alongside your medication. If you feel better, you may – with your doctor’s guidance – gradually reduce your medication while monitoring blood tests regularly.

How should I take BioEdge™?

I recommend taking 2 capsules after your second meal of the day with a glass of water.

How is BioEdge™ different from essential amino acids?

Essential amino acids are helpful but not enough on their own. They don’t support the liver. BioEdge™ includes the key amino acids needed to produce glutathione (crucial for T4 to T3 conversion) plus powerful liver-supporting ingredients like milk thistle, artichoke, dandelion root and choline.

How long does it take to work?

Most customers feel an improvement after about 3 days. Full effect develops after around 2 months.

How long does one jar last?

One jar contains 60 capsules and lasts exactly 30 days.

Is there a guarantee?

Yes, the manufacturer offers a 30-day money-back guarantee. Try it risk-free – if you’re not 100% convinced, simply email to info@thebioedge.co .

Although the company is still young, delivery was fast, customer service was helpful, and the product page includes verified customer reviews. They also regularly host Q&A sessions with thyroid experts.

כתב ויתור רפואי ובריאותי: המידע והתכנים האחרים המופיעים בדף זה, או בחומרים מקושרים כלשהם, אינם מיועדים ואין לפרש אותם כייעוץ רפואי, וגם אינם מהווים תחליף לייעוץ מקצועי רפואי או טיפול מקצועי. אם יש לך או לכל אדם אחר בעיה רפואית, עליך להתייעץ עם ספק שירותי הבריאות שלך או לפנות לטיפול רפואי מקצועי אחר. לעולם אל תתעלם מייעוץ רפואי מקצועי או תדחה את חיפושו בגלל משהו שקראת בדף זה או בחומרים מקושרים כלשהם. אם אתה חושב שיש לך מצב חירום רפואי, פנה מיד לרופא שלך או לשירותי החירום.
